transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Well, Dr. [Name], it's... it's a whole mess, honestly, and I just couldn't take it anymore. I came in today because of my husband's sister. She's been—well, she's been working this family business, right? And I don't mean just helping out. I mean she's been maneuvering, calculating every little thing she does. It's been going on for over a year now, more than a year of me watching her slowly try to get total control of the money. 

And it's not just the money, it's about pushing me out. She wants me completely out of any decisions, making sure my voice doesn't count for anything in my own family. My husband and the others, they keep trying to smooth it over, telling me I'm misreading things or that she's just "being helpful," but I know what I've been seeing. I've been watching her every move, the way she looks at the accounts, the way she talks over me when financial things come up. They can try to brush it under the rug all they want, but a person knows when they're being pushed out of their own life, you know? I just... I know exactly what she's doing.

Aside from what's going on with your sister-in-law, would you say you generally have a hard time trusting other people in your life—like friends, coworkers, or other family members—and has that been a pattern for you going back many years?

No, no, it's nothing like that at all. I'm actually a very open person, you know? I've never been the type to look over my shoulder or second-guess people. Take my neighbor, Sarah, for instance. We've lived next to each other for, oh, it has to be fifteen years now, and we leave our spare keys under each other's flower pots. I mean, if I had a hard time trusting people, I certainly wouldn't do that, right? And my friends from my old church group, we tell each other everything. I've always taken people at their word. That's just how I was raised. You look a person in the eye, and you believe them. 

So, no, I don't have some lifelong issue with trusting people. I've always gotten along fine with everyone. That's exactly what makes this whole situation with my husband's sister so incredibly frustrating! Because I *did* trust her in the beginning. When she first started coming around the business, I thought, "Oh, how nice, family helping family." I even made her a casserole when she was working late that first month. I was welcoming her with open arms. 

But then... well, then you start noticing the little things. You'd have to be blind not to. It started with the way she’d close the ledger the second I walked into the room. Just snap it shut. Or how she suddenly started handling the vendor payments without running it by me, and when I asked her about it, she gave me this... this smile that didn't reach her eyes and said she was "saving me the headache." Saving me the headache! It's not that I'm suspicious of people in general, Doctor, it's that I am actually paying attention to *her*. Anyone else in my shoes, if they saw the way she hovers over the bank deposit slips and whispers to my husband when she thinks I'm not listening, they'd know exactly what she's up to. It's just her. She's the one doing this.
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that others around you couldn't hear or see?

Heavens, no. No, nothing like that at all. I know sometimes when people come in to see a doctor like you, they might be... well, you know, dealing with things like that, hearing the television talk to them or seeing ghosts or whatever it is people go through. But my mind is sharp as a tack. I've never had any of that. 

I mean, I might not have finished high school—I had to leave in the eleventh grade to help my mother out at home, which is just how things were for my family back then—but I have always had perfect common sense. I rely on what's real. So when I tell you I hear things, I mean I hear real things. Like when I hear whispering, it's because my sister-in-law is actually standing right there in the hallway, physically whispering to my husband while I'm in the kitchen making lunch. I'm not hearing voices in the wind, I'm hearing her actual voice, trying to turn him against me. 

And my eyes work perfectly fine, too. I only see what is right there in plain daylight. Like I was saying about the business ledger, I saw her physically slam it shut with her own two hands. There wasn't some phantom doing it, it was her. I don't imagine things, Doctor. I really don't. Everything I'm telling you is just... well, it's just the plain old truth of what's happening right in front of my face. I've always been a very grounded person. So, no, no voices or visions or anything out of the ordinary like that. Just the very real sound of her trying to push me out of my own family.

Aside from this situation with your sister-in-law, has your daily life—your work, your relationships with others, your ability to manage your usual routines—stayed pretty much the same as always, or have you noticed changes in those areas too?

Oh, everything else is just exactly the same. I haven't let her disrupt my actual day-to-day life, if that's what you mean. I mean, I still keep up with my quilting group every Tuesday morning. We've been working on this beautiful double wedding ring pattern for the spring charity auction, and I wouldn't miss it for the world. And my choir practice on Thursday evenings, I'm still doing that, singing alto just like I have for the last ten years. 

Oh, and I've even kept up with my GED lessons! I go to the community center for those on Mondays and Wednesdays, because like I said earlier, I had to leave school in the eleventh grade to help my mother, and I just decided it was finally time to get that piece of paper. The instructor there is so patient with us. Plus, I still do my senior walks in the park with the ladies on Friday mornings. We do two miles, rain or shine, so my routine is very full and very normal. I keep myself active.

Really, the only thing this whole mess has changed is... well, obviously, how much I trust my husband's sister. That trust is completely gone, just shattered. And because of her, it's really changed which family gatherings I feel comfortable going to. I used to love going to all the Sunday dinners and the holiday cookouts, but now I have to stop and think before I RSVP. I have to ask myself, 'Is she going to be there?' Because if she is, I know she's going to be sitting across the table, watching me, whispering to my husband while I'm passing the potato salad, trying to make me look like I don't belong. I just can't stomach it. 

I actually skipped my own niece's birthday party last month because I knew my sister-in-law would be hovering around, trying to run the whole show and make me look irrelevant. It breaks my heart to miss out on family things, it really does, because I love my nieces and nephews, but I just can't be in the same room with that woman when I know what she's doing behind my back. So outside of avoiding her at family events, no, my life is completely normal. I stay busy, and I certainly don't let her take away my quilting or my choir!

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a fixed, encapsulated delusional belief (>1 year duration) that her sister-in-law is conspiring to steal family business finances and alienate her from the family, without any hallucinations, disorganized thought, or bizarre content. The belief is circumscribed to this specific persecutory/jealous theme, with no evidence of a pervasive, longstanding pattern of distrust (ruling out paranoid personality disorder) and no other psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations or thought disorder (ruling out schizophrenia). Functioning outside the delusional theme (quilting, choir, GED classes, walking group) remains intact, consistent with delusional disorder rather than a more pervasive psychotic or personality disorder.
